newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka troops consolidate after slow advance.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka troops consolidate after slow advance.

text.p: Sri Lankan security forces consolidated in captured northern rebel territory on Thursday after a slow two-day advance along one flank, the Defence Ministry and military officials said.
"Troops continue to strengthen their defences and dominate areas ahead of defences in Nedunkeni and Omanthai," a Defence Ministry statement said.

Military officials in the north said troops, who slowly resumed their drive into the rebels' northern Wanni stronghold on Tuesday after a six-day pause, had pushed further north of Omanthai, edging closer to the heavily fortified rebel town of Puliyankulam.
They said the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) had vacated at least two bases that lay along the path government troops were taking as they edged north.
"The LTTE have withdrawn. But when they come to an opportune place, they will engage the troops," one official told Reuters.

The army captured Nedunkeni, 40 km (25 miles) northeast of the government-controlled frontline town of Vavuniya, and Omanthai, 14 km (nine miles) north of Vavuniya, after a massive offensive launched last month. Vavuniya is 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo.
The military launched Operation Jaya Sikuru, or "Sure of Victory", from Vavuniya on May 13 in a bid to open a supply route to the Jaffna peninsula, 100 km (60 miles) further north.

Deputy Defence Minister Anuruddha Ratwatte told parliament on Thursday that the government was determined to go ahead with its plans to reopen the land route through the Wanni, linking Jaffna peninsula with the rest of the country.
The north-south highway has been closed for more than 10 years due to fighting between the rebels and government forces.
Ratwatte was speaking during a debate to extend the emergency regulations that govern the country by another month.
The Defence Ministry said on Thursday that rebels fired mortars at the army's forward defences on Wednesday and troops retaliated with mortar and artillery fire.
But the LTTE, fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in mainly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east, accused the military of a systematic demolition of Tamil towns.

A overnight statement issued by the LTTE's London office said the military was firing artillery at thickly-populated towns 32 km (20) miles away from its forward defences, forcing civilians to abandon their homes and seek refuge in jungles.
"Civilians are disoriented, frightened and hungry. Yet there has been no let-up in the shell-fire," the statement said.
The military denied their shells were aimed at civilians, claiming they only took on identified rebel targets.
"This is the LTTE's usual form. When security forces are on the offensive, they put out false stories about suffering civilians," a military spokesman in Colombo said.
Independent confirmation of the events was not possible as the international media has not been allowed in the war zone.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed since the war began in 1983. The rebels say the toll is higher.
